subject: databases
title: PostgreSQL
summary: A practical guide to Postgres: architecture, schema design, transactions, JSONB, indexing, vacuum, replication and recovery.

lessons.title: Clients, backends and connection pools
lessons.summary: Every client talks to its own server process, and the server enforces the rules for all of them.
lessons.body:
PostgreSQL, usually called **Postgres**, is an open-source relational database server. SQL is the language you send it; Postgres is the system that stores rows, enforces constraints, coordinates concurrent sessions and recovers after a crash. It also supports JSON documents, extensible types and PostgreSQL extensions, but those features do not remove the need to design your data carefully.

This module follows a small ticket shop through schema design, concurrency, indexing, maintenance and recovery. Read the SQL fundamentals first. The examples were run on PostgreSQL 18.6. In October 2026, 18 was the current major release and PostgreSQL 19 had reached its first release candidate, so check the release notes for changed defaults when you upgrade. Plans and timings depend on your data and installation. Run them in a fresh, disposable database, never an application database.

## Follow a database request

Your application uses a database driver to connect to the server. `psql` is another client: a terminal for sending SQL and inspecting the results. An ORM is a layer above a driver; it does not replace the database. Because every client ends up talking to the same server, rules such as constraints and row locking are enforced there, for all clients, including ones that bypass your ORM.

A PostgreSQL **database cluster** means a collection of databases managed by one server installation. It does not necessarily involve several machines. A connection selects one database. Inside it, PostgreSQL schemas such as `public` are namespaces containing tables, functions and other objects. `public.orders` names a table in a PostgreSQL schema, not a different database.

Postgres starts a separate **backend process** for each client connection. A supervisor process accepts the connection and starts the backend, which then parses, plans and executes that client's SQL. Backends share memory and coordinate access to storage. Starting a process per connection costs time and memory, so applications normally use a connection pool: a bounded set of open connections that requests borrow and return.

A typical request follows this path; responses travel back to the client:

```flow
Application sends parameterised SQL
Driver obtains a pooled connection
Postgres backend plans and executes
Result returns through the driver
Connection returns to the pool
```

The server's connection limit, `max_connections`, defaults to 100. Raising it is not a substitute for measuring CPU, memory, lock waits and throughput: each backend uses memory of its own, and many more active backends than CPU cores mostly compete for the same CPU, memory and locks.

With transaction pooling, an external pooler gives each transaction whichever server connection is free, so the next transaction may use a different backend process. Do not assume session settings or temporary objects will persist on the connection your application receives next.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a restaurant with dedicated waiters
> In this restaurant, every table that sits down gets its own waiter, who takes the order to a shared kitchen. Hiring and training a new waiter for every walk-in diner is slow, so a busy restaurant keeps a fixed team and seats parties at whichever waiter is free.
>
> **How it maps:** each waiter is a backend process serving one connection; the shared kitchen is the shared memory and storage. Keeping a fixed team is a connection pool. Seating a party with a different waiter for each course is transaction pooling, so a note left with the first waiter (a session setting or temporary table) may not reach the next.
>
> **Where it stops:** real waiters often cover several tables, but a backend serves exactly one connection for its whole life. Hiring more waiters helps a restaurant until the kitchen is full; with Postgres, extra backends compete for the same CPU, memory and locks, so throughput can fall.

To connect to a database that already exists locally:

```sh
psql -d postgres_study
```

Inside `psql`, `\conninfo` shows the connection, `\dt` lists tables and `\d events` describes a table. SQL statements end with a semicolon; these backslash commands are client commands. Use a PostgreSQL non-superuser role for the application with only the required database privileges, and bind user values through driver parameters rather than joining them into SQL strings.

## Key takeaways

- The server enforces constraints and row locking for every client, not the ORM or pool.
- Each connection gets its own backend process, so pools reuse a bounded number of them.
- A cluster can be one server installation holding several databases.
- Transaction pooling means session state may not follow your next transaction.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: architectural fundamentals](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/tutorial-arch.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: how connections are established](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/connect-estab.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: psql](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/app-psql.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: role attributes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/role-attributes.html)

questions.prompt: Your web app uses an ORM, a driver and PostgreSQL. Where are foreign keys and concurrent row updates enforced?

options.text: In the ORM only
options.explanation: Another client can bypass the ORM, so database invariants cannot depend on it alone.

options.text: In the PostgreSQL server
options.explanation: The server applies constraints and concurrency rules to operations from all clients.

options.text: In psql
options.explanation: psql is a client, not the storage and concurrency engine.

options.text: In the connection pool
options.explanation: A pool reuses connections; it does not enforce relational constraints.

questions.workedExample:
1. The ORM produces operations and the driver sends them.
2. The pool provides a connection.
3. The server executes the SQL, checks constraints and coordinates conflicting writes.

lessons.title: Ticket schema, constraints and types
lessons.summary: Put the shop's rules in constraints and pick types for what values mean.
lessons.body:
Build the ticket-shop fixture in a fresh disposable PostgreSQL database. The SQL was run on PostgreSQL 18 and also runs on versions 16 and 17. Later units reuse these exact two tables.

## Enforce rules beside the data

Create two tables. An event has available seats; a booking refers to an event and has an application-supplied request key.

```sql
-- Event-level invariants live here.
CREATE TABLE events (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
    PRIMARY KEY,
  name text NOT NULL,
  seats_left integer NOT NULL
    CHECK (seats_left >= 0),
  starts_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  details jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'
);

-- UNIQUE identifies repeated requests.
CREATE TABLE bookings (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
    PRIMARY KEY,
  event_id bigint NOT NULL
    REFERENCES events(id),
  request_key text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL
    DEFAULT now()
);
```

The identity column generates values, while `PRIMARY KEY` enforces uniqueness. Generated IDs can have gaps, including after an aborted transaction; do not interpret the highest ID as the number of rows. If IDs must be created outside the database, PostgreSQL 18 adds `uuidv7()`, which makes time-ordered UUIDs; an identity column is simpler when the database creates every row. A foreign key prevents a booking for a missing event. `CHECK` rejects negative availability, and `NOT NULL` separately rejects an unknown value: a check expression evaluating to NULL does not reject the row.

The unique request key will help identify retries of the same booking. Enforcing this in the database closes the race in which two requests both check for an existing key, find none, then insert duplicates.

Postgres automatically creates an index for a primary key or unique constraint. It does **not** automatically index the referencing side of every foreign key. Later, we will add an index starting with `bookings.event_id` to support lookups by event.

### Choose types for their meaning

| Value | Useful type | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| A count | `integer` | Exact whole number |
| A monetary amount | `numeric(12,2)` | Exact decimal arithmetic |
| An event instant | `timestamptz` | Represents a point in time |
| Optional attributes | `jsonb` | Queryable structured document |

`timestamptz` converts input to an instant and displays it in the session time zone. It does not preserve the original zone name. A recurring “9am Europe/London” schedule needs the named zone and scheduling rules as well as individual occurrence instants. For money, record the currency too; a decimal type cannot tell pounds from euros.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a live broadcast in TV listings
> A summer football final kicks off once, at one moment. A London listings page prints it at 20:00 and a Tokyo page prints it at 04:00 the next morning. Neither listing records which city first announced the time. A weekly show "every Monday at 9am London time" is a different kind of fact: a rule that must follow the UK's clock changes.
>
> **How it maps:** the kick-off is the instant `timestamptz` stores. Each listing page is a session time zone, which changes only how the instant is displayed. The weekly rule is the named zone plus recurrence information you must store separately.
>
> **Where it stops:** a listings page can print any format it likes, but `timestamptz` stores nothing except the instant: it keeps no zone name and no original offset, and converts to the session's zone only when it displays the value.

Insert the first event and inspect the generated ID:

```sql
-- RETURNING gives the generated ID.
INSERT INTO events
  (name, seats_left, starts_at, details)
VALUES (
  'Postgres workshop',
  2,
  '2027-05-01 10:00:00+00',
  '{"format":"online"}'
)
RETURNING id, seats_left;
```

In this fresh database the ID is 1. In an application, use the returned ID instead of assuming it. `RETURNING` avoids a separate query to discover which row was created.

## Key takeaways

- Use NOT NULL as well as a CHECK: a CHECK that evaluates to NULL does not reject the row.
- Identity generates values; a primary key enforces uniqueness.
- `timestamptz` stores an instant; recurrence rules and zone names need their own columns.
- Foreign keys do not get an index automatically on the referencing side.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: identity columns](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-identity-columns.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: date/time types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/datatype-datetime.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: numeric types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/datatype-numeric.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: UUID functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/functions-uuid.html)

questions.prompt: A required seats_left column must never be negative or unknown. Which definition enforces both requirements?

options.text: integer CHECK (seats_left >= 0)
options.explanation: CHECK alone accepts a NULL result, so NULL can still be stored.

options.text: integer DEFAULT 0
options.explanation: A default supplies an omitted value but does not reject explicit NULL or negative input.

options.text: integer UNIQUE
options.explanation: Uniqueness does not enforce the allowed range or reject NULL.

options.text: integer NOT NULL CHECK (seats_left >= 0)
options.explanation: NOT NULL rejects unknown values and CHECK rejects negative values.

questions.workedExample:
1. Test -1: the check is false, so insertion fails.
2. Test NULL: NOT NULL rejects it.
3. Test 0: both constraints pass. Each constraint contributes a distinct rule.

questions.prompt: You store an event instant as timestamptz. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Its displayed time can change with the session time zone
options.explanation: Postgres renders the stored instant in the session time zone.

options.text: It preserves the original named time zone automatically
options.explanation: It preserves an instant, not the input zone name.

options.text: A recurring 9am London schedule needs additional zone and recurrence information
options.explanation: One instant does not encode future occurrences or daylight-saving rules.

options.text: It is an appropriate exact decimal type for a ticket price
options.explanation: Use a numeric decimal type or a deliberate minor-unit representation for amounts, not a timestamp.

questions.workedExample:
1. Separate an instant from a local clock reading.
2. The same instant can display differently in London and Tokyo.
3. Future 9am London occurrences require a named zone and recurrence rules, not merely the first occurrence.

lessons.title: Reserve the last seat safely
lessons.summary: Put the availability check inside the UPDATE so two buyers cannot both win the last seat.
lessons.body:
The ticket-shop fixture has `events(id bigint PRIMARY KEY, seats_left integer NOT NULL CHECK (seats_left >= 0))`, plus the name, start time and JSONB columns introduced in the schema unit. Use the returned event-table ID; the fresh ticket-shop fixture below assumes event 1 exists.

## Make the decision inside the write

An unsafe application reads `seats_left = 1`, checks it in application code and later writes `seats_left = 0`. Two clients can both read 1 and both claim success. Wrapping that read and write in a default transaction alone does not fix the race, because each SELECT simply reads the latest committed value without reserving anything.

Instead, combine the condition and change in one statement:

```sql
-- Only a row with seats can change.
UPDATE events
SET seats_left = seats_left - 1
WHERE id = 1 AND seats_left > 0
RETURNING id, seats_left;
-- No returned row means no reservation.
```

A returned row means a seat was reserved. No returned row means no matching event with available seats, so the application must check the row count before telling the customer anything.

Why only one buyer can win: an UPDATE locks each row it changes until its transaction ends. Under Read Committed, the default, a second transaction updating the same row waits for that lock. When the first commits, the second re-evaluates its `WHERE` condition against the newly committed row. Starting with one seat, the first changes 1 to 0, the second rechecks `seats_left > 0`, finds it false and updates nothing.

At Repeatable Read the waiting transaction does not recheck. Once the first commits, it fails with "could not serialize access due to concurrent update", and the application must retry the whole transaction. Both levels prevent the double booking; they differ in what the loser sees.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: one ticket left at the box office
> Two fans see "1 left" on a website and both drive to the box office. If each one's decision was made at home, both believe they have a ticket. If the clerk only hands over a ticket after checking the drawer at the moment of sale, the second fan is told "sold out".
>
> **How it maps:** deciding at home is reading `seats_left` in application code and writing later. The clerk checking the drawer during the sale is the `WHERE seats_left > 0` condition inside the UPDATE. Queueing at the single window is the row lock that makes the second transaction wait.
>
> **Where it stops:** the clerk sees the drawer change as it happens. A waiting transaction under Read Committed rechecks only that row's new committed version, and under Repeatable Read it gets an error instead of a "sold out" answer.

PostgreSQL 18 also lets `RETURNING` name the old and new values, for example `RETURNING old.seats_left, new.seats_left`, which is handy for audit messages. Earlier versions return only the new values from an UPDATE.

## Key takeaways

- Combine the availability test and the decrement in one UPDATE.
- At Read Committed a waiting updater rechecks the committed row; at Repeatable Read it gets a serialization error instead.
- Check the returned row count before claiming success.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: transaction isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/transaction-iso.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: UPDATE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-update.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: explicit locking](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/explicit-locking.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: returning data from modified rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/dml-returning.html)

questions.prompt: One seat remains. Two Read Committed transactions run a conditional UPDATE that subtracts 1 only where seats_left > 0. Both eventually commit. What happens?

options.text: Both succeed because both initially saw 1
options.explanation: A conflicting updater waits and rechecks the row condition after the other commits.

options.text: The count becomes -1 unless isolation is Serializable
options.explanation: The condition and same-row write coordination prevent the second decrement here.

options.text: One update returns a row; the other returns no row
options.explanation: After the first changes 1 to 0, the second rechecks seats_left > 0 and finds it false.

options.text: Ordinary SELECT statements must be blocked until both finish
options.explanation: MVCC allows ordinary reads of visible row versions; it does not require this blanket blocking.

questions.workedExample:
1. Transaction A updates the row from 1 to 0 and holds the row lock.
2. B waits for A.
3. After A commits, B rechecks the condition against 0.
4. The condition fails, so B cannot claim a seat. The application must inspect the returned row count.

lessons.title: Booking retries and rollback
lessons.summary: Commit the seat and the booking together, and make a retry find the first booking instead of taking another seat.
lessons.body:
Use the ticket-shop `events` and `bookings` tables from the schema unit in a disposable database. Event 1 must exist with at least one seat. `bookings.event_id` references the event; `request_key` is NOT NULL and UNIQUE. Each new logical booking receives its own request key.

## Commit the whole booking or none

To reserve and record a booking atomically, use a transaction. This example is for a new request key and assumes the update returns one row:

```sql
-- Both database changes must commit.
BEGIN;

-- Only a row with seats can change.
UPDATE events
SET seats_left = seats_left - 1
WHERE id = 1 AND seats_left > 0
RETURNING id;

-- Proceed only if UPDATE returned a row.
INSERT INTO bookings
  (event_id, request_key)
VALUES (1, 'request-001')
RETURNING id;

COMMIT;
```

The application must inspect the update result. If it returns no rows, issue `ROLLBACK` and do not insert the booking. If the insert fails, roll back the transaction so the seat decrement is undone. An SQL error normally leaves the transaction aborted until rollback, unless you recover using a savepoint.

For a duplicate request key, roll back and then fetch the existing booking, checking that it belongs to the same intended request. Do **not** decrement a seat, use `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` for the booking and then commit regardless: the duplicate insert might do nothing while the extra decrement persists. A unique key is a building block for idempotency, not a complete workflow.

Keep transactions short. Do not hold the row lock while waiting for a customer or payment provider. External effects need their own retry design and checks to resolve uncertain payment outcomes; an SQL rollback does not undo a payment request to an external service.

## Key takeaways

- Roll back if the reservation returns no row or the insert fails.
- A duplicate insert must not leave an extra decrement committed.
- Database rollback cannot reverse an external payment.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: INSERT and ON CONFLICT](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-insert.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: transactions tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/tutorial-transactions.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: SAVEPOINT](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-savepoint.html)

questions.prompt: A retry decrements a seat, then INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING skips an existing booking request key. The application commits. What is the bug?

options.text: The extra decrement can commit without a new booking
options.explanation: DO NOTHING affects the conflicting insert, not the earlier successful UPDATE.

options.text: Postgres automatically rolls back every statement when DO NOTHING skips a row
options.explanation: Skipping a conflicting insert is not a transaction error.

options.text: The unique constraint has stopped working
options.explanation: The constraint prevented a duplicate booking exactly as intended.

options.text: RETURNING would itself undo the decrement
options.explanation: RETURNING reports affected rows; it does not reverse earlier writes.

questions.workedExample:
1. Suppose seats_left starts at 5.
2. The retry changes it to 4.
3. The insert skips the duplicate key.
4. COMMIT keeps 4 even though no booking was added. Roll back the duplicate attempt and retrieve the existing booking, checking request identity.

lessons.title: Snapshots, write skew and retries
lessons.summary: A stable snapshot does not stop two transactions breaking a rule across different rows.
lessons.body:
Postgres uses **MVCC**: updates create new row versions, and snapshots decide which versions a query can see. Ordinary reads generally do not block ordinary writes, but writers updating the same row can block each other. Schema changes and explicit locks introduce other conflicts.

| Isolation | Read behaviour | Remaining responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Read Committed | New snapshot per statement | Protect multi-step decisions |
| Repeatable Read | Stable transaction snapshot | Handle write skew and retries |
| Serializable | Successful work matches a one-at-a-time order | Retry aborted transactions |

Read Committed is the default. Two SELECTs in one transaction can see different committed values. Repeatable Read keeps a snapshot from its first non-transaction-control statement, but it is not equivalent to serial transaction execution. At every level, a transaction can see its own prior writes.

Imagine two on-call staff, both active. Each transaction sees two active staff and marks a different person inactive. At Repeatable Read, they can update different rows and both commit, breaking the rule that someone must remain on call. This is **write skew**. Use a suitable shared locking protocol or Serializable transactions for all operations maintaining that rule. Under Serializable, PostgreSQL tracks what each transaction read as well as what it wrote, so it notices the cross-row conflict and makes one of the two fail with SQLSTATE `40001`, sometimes not until it tries to commit.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: two people reading one photo of the rota
> Asha and Ben each take a photo of the on-call whiteboard, see two names, and each walks away to rub out their own name. Neither touches the other's name, so nobody notices a clash, and the board ends up empty.
>
> **How it maps:** each photo is a Repeatable Read snapshot taken at the start. Rubbing out different names is updating different rows, which causes no same-row lock conflict. The empty board is the broken "someone must be on call" invariant.
>
> **Where it stops:** a photo really is a separate copy; a snapshot is just a rule about which row versions a query may see. Serializable has no whiteboard equivalent: it records read and write dependencies and cancels one participant when it detects a dangerous pattern.

When a transaction fails with `40001`, retry the **whole transaction**, including its reads and decisions, with a bounded retry policy. Retrying only the last statement can reuse a decision based on an obsolete snapshot. Deadlocks can also require a transaction retry; acquire multiple row locks in a consistent order to reduce them.

For a more involved read-then-change operation, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` can lock the selected rows. It does not lock an imaginary row that does not exist, so use constraints or a suitable isolation strategy for “insert if absent” rules.

## Key takeaways

- A stable snapshot does not prevent write skew.
- Serializable participants must retry the whole failed transaction.
- Locking existing rows does not lock an absent row.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: transaction isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/transaction-iso.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: explicit locking](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/explicit-locking.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: serialization failure handling](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html)

questions.prompt: Two Repeatable Read transactions each see two on-call staff, then each marks a different person inactive. Both commit. Which explanation and remedy fit?

options.text: Repeatable Read permits write skew; use Serializable with whole-transaction retries or a suitable shared locking protocol
options.explanation: Stable snapshots alone do not prevent conflicting decisions that write different rows.

options.text: This is a dirty read; Repeatable Read allows uncommitted data
options.explanation: Repeatable Read does not allow dirty reads.

options.text: A separate index on each name makes the invariant serializable
options.explanation: An access-path index does not enforce the cross-row on-call rule.

options.text: Retry only COMMIT after a serialization failure
options.explanation: The transaction must restart and reconsider its reads and decisions.

questions.workedExample:
1. Both snapshots show a second active person.
2. The transactions modify different rows, so no same-row conflict stops them.
3. Together they violate the invariant.
4. Coordinate the shared rule, or use Serializable for its participants and retry any rejected transaction from the beginning.

lessons.title: Choose indexes and read the plan
lessons.summary: Match the index method and column order to the query, then check the plan on realistic data.
lessons.body:
Use the ticket-shop fixture: `bookings` has an identity primary key `id`, an `event_id` foreign key, a unique `request_key`, and a `created_at timestamptz` column. Create the tables in the schema unit first; populate representative data for meaningful performance measurements.

## Match an index to the request

Suppose an admin page needs an event's latest bookings:

```sql
-- Filter by event, then read newest first.
CREATE INDEX bookings_event_recent
ON bookings (event_id, created_at DESC);

SELECT id, created_at
FROM bookings
WHERE event_id = 1
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

This B-tree index puts the equality filter first and the requested ordering second. Postgres can jump to one event's entries, read them already in newest-first order and stop after 20, without sorting all that event's bookings. Column order matters: an index on `(created_at, event_id)` keeps entries in time order across all events, so one event's bookings are scattered through it.

In a test run on PostgreSQL 18 with 400,000 bookings spread over 52 events, this query touched only about a dozen pages (index plus table) and needed no Sort. With the index dropped, the planner scanned the whole 2,942-page table and sorted that event's roughly 7,700 matching rows to keep the newest 20.

The index costs storage, and writes must keep it up to date. Adding one to every column is rarely a good trade.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a filing cabinet with a drawer per event
> Picture a cabinet with one drawer per event, each drawer's folders filed newest first. To fetch an event's latest 20 bookings, you open one drawer and lift out the front 20 folders. A cabinet filed purely by date would make you search every drawer for that event's folders.
>
> **How it maps:** the drawer is the leading `event_id` column; the folder order inside it is `created_at DESC`. Lifting the front 20 is the Index Scan feeding `LIMIT 20` with no Sort.
>
> **Where it stops:** a B-tree is a tree of index pages, not drawers, and the planner may still decide a plain table scan is cheaper. Postgres can also read an index backwards: the same index served `ORDER BY created_at ASC` for one event with an Index Scan Backward.

PostgreSQL 18 added **skip scan**: a multicolumn B-tree can sometimes serve a condition on a later column alone by searching once per distinct leading value. In the test above, a filter on `created_at` alone used this index with 53 index searches, one for each event plus one. That works well when the leading column has only a few different values; with many, a separate index on the later column is still the better fit.

Different index methods suit different operators:

- **B-tree** is the usual choice for equality, ranges and ordered retrieval.
- **GIN** supports inverted lookups, including many JSONB and full-text search operations.
- **GiST** suits overlap and nearness questions, such as range types and geometric data.
- **BRIN** stores summaries over page ranges; it can be compact and useful when values correlate with physical order, such as append-heavy timestamp data. Candidate pages still need rechecking.

A sequential scan is not automatically bad: reading most rows, or a tiny table, can be cheaper than visiting an index and fetching rows from the table heap. On the tiny example table, the planner ignores the index and sorts.

## Read the plan

Use the **Query Processing & Optimisation** lessons for deeper plan analysis. Start with this diagnostic on representative data:

```sql
-- This executes the SELECT below.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, created_at
FROM bookings
WHERE event_id = 1
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

`EXPLAIN` estimates a plan; its `ANALYZE` option actually executes it. In PostgreSQL 18, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` reports buffers even without the `BUFFERS` option; writing it keeps the command working the same way on older versions. Costs are planner units, not milliseconds. Compare estimated versus actual row counts, inspect repeated loops, and look at buffer activity before changing settings. A shared-buffer read can still be served from the OS page cache, so it is not proof of a physical disk read. Do not add up inclusive timings of parents and children.

> [!warning] ANALYZE has two meanings
> `ANALYZE bookings` updates planner statistics. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the supplied query and measures execution, including writes if the query modifies data. Use a disposable database for write experiments; even rollback does not undo sequence increments or external side effects.

## Key takeaways

- Put equality columns first and the ordering column next in a composite B-tree.
- Choose the index method by operator: B-tree, GIN, GiST or BRIN.
- PostgreSQL 18 skip scan helps only when the leading column has few different values.
- A tiny or unselective query can still favour a sequential scan.
- EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes; buffer reads need not be disk reads.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: index types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-types.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: multicolumn indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-multicolumn.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: indexes and ORDER BY](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-ordering.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: using EXPLAIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/using-explain.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: EXPLAIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-explain.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: BRIN indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/brin.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/release-18.html)

questions.prompt: An admin page filters bookings by event_id and orders them by created_at DESC with LIMIT 20. Which index best matches that access pattern?

options.text: A GIN index on events.details
options.explanation: That serves document queries on another table, not the booking filter and order.

options.text: A B-tree on (event_id, created_at DESC)
options.explanation: Equality on the first column restricts the range, and the next column supplies the requested order.

options.text: A unique index on created_at

lessons.title: JSONB alongside relational columns
lessons.summary: Keep required values and relationships in typed columns, and use JSONB for attributes that genuinely vary.
lessons.body:
The ticket-shop `events` table has `name text NOT NULL` and `details jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'`, alongside its identity, availability and start-time columns. The schema unit inserts a workshop with `{ "format": "online" }` in `details`. Run the following queries after that ticket-shop fixture setup.

## Keep important rules explicit

Use relational columns for important keys, relationships and invariants. Use JSONB for attributes that genuinely vary, such as event presentation settings.

```sql
-- Match a contained key/value pair.
SELECT name
FROM events
WHERE details @> '{"format":"online"}';

-- GIN can index containment searches.
CREATE INDEX events_details_gin
ON events USING gin (details);
```

The containment operator `@>` asks whether the document includes the given keys and values. A GIN index can serve it for selective queries at sufficient scale. In a PostgreSQL 18 test with 200,000 documents, a search matching 200 of them used the GIN index, while a search matching almost every row ignored it and scanned the table. An ordinary B-tree index on the whole `jsonb` column does not help `@>` at all, because index support depends on the operator and the index method.

JSONB stores a processed representation rather than the input text. It drops insignificant whitespace, does not keep key order, and keeps only the last value for a duplicated key: `'{"a": 2, "a": 3}'::jsonb` becomes `{"a": 3}`. Use `json` instead if preserving the input text matters more than JSONB's processing and indexing advantages.

A JSON document does not automatically enforce the types and relationships your application expects. If every event has a required capacity used in constraints and joins, a typed column is usually easier to validate and optimise than hiding it in JSON. Updating one key still writes a new version of the whole row, with its write and index maintenance costs.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a printed form with a notes section
> A booking form has printed boxes for name, date and number of seats, which a clerk checks before accepting it. At the bottom is a free notes section where people write whatever extra details they like.
>
> **How it maps:** the printed boxes are typed columns with `NOT NULL`, `CHECK` and foreign keys. The notes section is the JSONB column: flexible, but nobody checks that "capacity" was written there, or written as a number.
>
> **Where it stops:** handwritten notes are hard to search, whereas JSONB keeps typed JSON values that you can query and index with GIN. A notes section also keeps exactly what was written; JSONB normalises it.

## Key takeaways

- Keep required values and relationships in constrained columns.
- GIN can support selective JSONB containment queries; a plain B-tree cannot.
- JSONB drops whitespace, key order and all but the last duplicate key.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: JSON types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/datatype-json.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: GIN indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/gin.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: index types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/indexes-types.html)

questions.prompt: Events have variable presentation attributes in JSONB. Queries use details @> a small JSON object. Which approach is sensible?

options.text: Move all keys and foreign-key relationships into JSONB
options.explanation: That makes important relational invariants harder to express and enforce.

options.text: Expect JSONB to preserve original whitespace and key order
options.explanation: JSONB stores a processed representation, not the original input text.

options.text: Keep core invariants in typed columns and consider a GIN index for selective containment queries
options.explanation: This combines explicit schema rules with JSONB flexibility and an index suited to containment.

options.text: Add a B-tree and assume it accelerates every JSON operator
options.explanation: Index support depends on the operator and index method.

questions.workedExample:
1. Event identity and seat availability have stable meanings and constraints.
2. Optional presentation attributes can vary in JSONB.
3. For selective containment searches, evaluate a GIN index on representative data; it adds write and storage cost.

lessons.title: Vacuum, old snapshots and statistics
lessons.summary: Why update-heavy tables grow, what stops vacuum reclaiming space, and how to find the blocker.
lessons.body:
Every UPDATE in Postgres writes a new row version and leaves the old one behind; a DELETE leaves its version behind too. An old version cannot be removed while any transaction might still need to see it. Once no transaction can, it is a dead tuple.

**VACUUM** removes dead versions from tables and indexes and marks their space reusable for future rows. It also maintains visibility information and freezes old rows to prevent transaction ID wraparound, covered two units later. Plain vacuum normally reuses space inside the table rather than returning it to the operating system; it only gives back completely empty pages at the very end of the table.

**ANALYZE** samples data to update planner statistics. Postgres uses those estimates to choose scan and join strategies. Autovacuum runs both automatically; monitor whether it keeps up rather than treating it as optional background noise.

## Why a table bloats

A healthy update-heavy table settles at a stable size: its live rows plus the dead space that builds up between vacuum runs, which new versions keep reusing. It grows beyond that, which is called table bloat, when dead versions pile up faster than they are reclaimed. Two causes are common:

- Vacuum runs too rarely for the update rate, which the next unit's thresholds explain.
- Something holds back the **cleanup horizon**: the oldest point in time that some transaction might still need to see. Vacuum cannot remove a version that died after that point, however often it runs.

Long-running work holds the horizon back. The usual culprits are:

- a long-running query or transaction, including one left **idle in transaction** by an application that forgot to commit;
- a forgotten prepared transaction;
- a replication slot that still records an old `xmin` from a standby that has stopped connecting (a logical slot holds back only system-catalog cleanup and WAL);
- a standby with `hot_standby_feedback` on, running long queries.

The isolation level matters for an idle transaction. Under Read Committed, each statement takes a fresh snapshot and releases it when it finishes. A transaction that has only read and then sits idle holds no snapshot, so it does not block cleanup, although it may still hold locks. A Repeatable Read transaction keeps its snapshot until it ends. A transaction that has written anything holds a transaction ID, and that also holds the horizon back until it ends.

In a PostgreSQL 18 test, updating all 10,000 rows of a small table while another session sat in an idle Repeatable Read transaction left `VACUUM (VERBOSE)` reporting "0 removed … 10000 are dead but not yet removable". Three rounds of updates and vacuums nearly quadrupled the table from 360 kB to 1,416 kB. Once the old transaction ended, the next vacuum removed all 30,000 dead versions, but the file stayed at 1,416 kB; later updates reused that free space. Only `VACUUM FULL` shrank it back to 360 kB.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a library that keeps old editions for slow readers
> A library replaces its reference books with new editions but keeps each old edition on the shelf while anyone who borrowed the reading room before the change is still inside. One visitor who never leaves forces it to keep every edition published since they arrived, and the shelves fill up.
>
> **How it maps:** editions are row versions; the visitor who arrived earliest is the oldest snapshot, which sets the cleanup horizon. Clearing old editions onto a "free shelf space" list is plain VACUUM. Building a new, smaller bookcase and moving everything across is VACUUM FULL.
>
> **Where it stops:** the library knows exactly which visitor reads which book. Postgres does not track that: one old snapshot holds back cleanup of versions in every table of that database, whether or not it ever reads them, and the horizon also counts slots and standbys that are not readers at all.

## Find the blocker

Look for the oldest transactions holding a transaction ID or snapshot:

```sql
-- Oldest horizon holders first.
SELECT pid, state, xact_start,
       backend_xid, backend_xmin
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_xid IS NOT NULL
   OR backend_xmin IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY xact_start;
```

Also check `pg_prepared_xacts` for old prepared transactions and `pg_replication_slots` for slots with an old `xmin` or `catalog_xmin`. `pg_stat_user_tables` shows each table's estimated dead tuples and its last vacuum times. Ending the blocker lets the next vacuum clean up; `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` can end forgotten idle-in-transaction sessions automatically.

To vacuum and analyse one table by hand:

```sql
-- Run outside an explicit transaction.
VACUUM (ANALYZE) bookings;
```

Disabling autovacuum or routinely running `VACUUM FULL` is not a general fix. `VACUUM FULL` copies the table into a new file, needs extra disk space while it runs, and holds an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that blocks even reads of the table until it finishes.

An update can sometimes be a heap-only tuple (HOT) update, avoiding new ordinary index entries when no non-summarising indexed column changes and the original heap page has room. This reduces index maintenance and lets dead versions be pruned within the page; it does not remove the need for vacuum. Since PostgreSQL 16, summarising indexes such as BRIN do not by themselves disqualify HOT. Leaving free space in pages with a lower `fillfactor` makes HOT updates more likely.

## Key takeaways

- An update-heavy table bloats when dead versions pile up faster than vacuum reclaims them.
- Old snapshots, written-but-uncommitted transactions, prepared transactions and replication slots with an old `xmin` hold back cleanup.
- An idle Read Committed transaction that has only read does not hold a snapshot.
- Plain VACUUM makes space reusable; the file does not shrink. VACUUM FULL rewrites and strongly locks the table.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: routine vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/routine-vacuuming.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: VACUUM](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-vacuum.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: heap-only tuples](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/storage-hot.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: ANALYZE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-analyze.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: pg_stat_activity and statistics views](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/monitoring-stats.html)

questions.prompt: An update-heavy table keeps growing while an old transaction retains a snapshot. Which actions or explanations are sound? Select all that apply.

options.text: Disable autovacuum to stop it competing with writes
options.explanation: That can worsen dead-version accumulation and wraparound risk.

options.text: Investigate the old transaction because it may hold back removal of row versions
options.explanation: Versions still needed by a snapshot cannot yet be reclaimed.

options.text: Monitor autovacuum and distinguish reusable table space and space returned to the OS
options.explanation: Plain vacuum usually makes space reusable within the table.

options.text: Run VACUUM FULL routinely because it never blocks normal access
options.explanation: VACUUM FULL copies the table into a new file and requires a strong lock.

questions.workedExample:
1. Updates leave old versions.
2. An old snapshot may still need them.
3. Investigate why that transaction remains open and whether maintenance is keeping up.
4. Even after cleanup, reusable pages do not imply the table file immediately shrinks.

lessons.title: Understand autovacuum thresholds
lessons.summary: Autovacuum waits for dead versions in proportion to table size, so big busy tables often need their own settings.
lessons.body:
This unit uses PostgreSQL 18 defaults. PostgreSQL 16 and 17 have no `autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold` cap. These are eligibility thresholds, not promises that a worker starts immediately.

## Size-dependent cleanup

Autovacuum does not clean a table after every update. It waits until enough dead row versions have built up to make the work worthwhile, and that point grows with the table. The relationship is worth seeing because it explains why large tables are cleaned so rarely:

```formula essential
T_vac = min(T_max, T_base + sN)
where
T_vac: the vacuum threshold, in row versions (tuples): autovacuum vacuums the table once its estimated count of dead versions exceeds this
min: the minimum function: whichever of its two inputs is smaller
T_max: autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold, a cap added in PostgreSQL 18 so the threshold cannot grow without limit on huge tables; default 100,000,000 tuples
T_base: autovacuum_vacuum_threshold, a fixed base that matters only for tiny tables; default 50 tuples
s: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor, the fraction of the table's estimated row count added to the base; default 0.2 (20 %), no unit
N: the estimated number of rows in the table, kept in pg_class.reltuples and refreshed by VACUUM and ANALYZE
In words: by default a table becomes eligible once its dead versions exceed fifty plus a fifth of its rows, capped at one hundred million.
```

So the dead-version allowance scales with size. A 1,000-row table becomes eligible after about 250 dead versions; a 1,000,000-row table only after about 200,000; a 50-million-row table after about 10 million. The cap matters only beyond about 500 million rows. The count is of row versions, not distinct rows: updating the same row five times leaves five obsolete versions.

That proportion is why a large, busy table can bloat even though autovacuum is "working": millions of dead versions accumulate between runs, and the size the table settles at includes them. The usual fix is a smaller vacuum scale factor for that table alone, set as a storage parameter:

```sql
-- Vacuum after ~1% of rows are dead.
ALTER TABLE bookings
SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01);
```

## Eligible is not the same as started

The autovacuum launcher tries to start a worker in each database about once every `autovacuum_naptime`, one minute by default. At most `autovacuum_max_workers` (3 by default) run at once. If several large tables become eligible together, all workers can be busy for a long time and other eligible tables wait. Workers also pause briefly as they go (cost-based delay, 2 ms by default) to limit their I/O impact, so a single large vacuum can take a while.

Two similar rules start other work:

- Many inserts start a vacuum: by default once more than 1,000 rows plus 20 % of the rows in the part of the table not yet frozen have been inserted since the last vacuum. These vacuums let insert-only tables have pages marked all-visible and rows frozen before the work piles up.
- Enough changes start an ANALYZE: by default 50 rows plus 10 % of the table, counting inserts, updates and deletes.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a cleaner who visits by the size of the room
> An office cleaner comes to each room once a fifth of its desks have been left messy. A five-desk meeting room is cleaned after one messy desk; a 1,000-desk open-plan floor waits for 200. The cleaning company also has only three cleaners, who do a round of the building roughly once a minute.
>
> **How it maps:** the fraction of messy desks is the vacuum scale factor and the room size is the table's row count. Three cleaners are the default worker limit, and the round is the naptime. Telling the company to clean the big floor after ten messy desks is a per-table vacuum scale factor.
>
> **Where it stops:** a cleaner sees mess directly. Autovacuum works from estimated counts in the statistics system, a fixed base of 50 means tiny tables wait for more than the fraction alone suggests, and dead versions held back by an old snapshot stay uncleaned however often a worker visits.

## Key takeaways

- The dead-version threshold is a fixed base plus a fraction of the table, capped in PostgreSQL 18.
- Large tables accumulate many dead versions between runs; lower their vacuum scale factor per table.
- Eligibility does not guarantee an immediate start: naptime, worker limits and throttling matter.
- Separate thresholds cover insert-only tables and ANALYZE.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: routine vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/routine-vacuuming.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: autovacuum settings](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-autovacuum.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: vacuuming settings](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-vacuum.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: CREATE TABLE storage parameters](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-createtable.html)

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL 18 `bookings` table holds 50 million rows and takes steady updates. With default settings, autovacuum only becomes eligible after about 10 million dead row versions, and the table keeps bloating between runs. Which change most directly makes autovacuum clean this table sooner?

options.text: Set `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01` on this table
options.explanation: Correct. The threshold is mostly the vacuum scale factor times the row count, so dropping it from 20 % to 1 % for this table makes it eligible after about 500,000 dead versions instead of about 10 million, without changing other tables.

options.text: Raise `autovacuum_vacuum_threshold` from 50 to 1,000
options.explanation: The fixed base is negligible beside 20 % of 50 million rows, and raising it would make autovacuum wait slightly longer, not sooner.

options.text: Increase `autovacuum_naptime` so each check is more thorough
options.explanation: Naptime is the gap between the launcher's rounds. A longer gap makes eligible tables wait longer; it does not change how many dead versions are needed.

options.text: Disable autovacuum and run VACUUM FULL every night
options.explanation: This lets dead versions build up all day and also stops automatic ANALYZE, and VACUUM FULL rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that blocks reads and writes while it runs.

questions.workedExample:
1. The eligibility threshold is a fixed base (50) plus the vacuum scale factor (20 %) of the estimated row count, capped at 100 million in PostgreSQL 18.
2. For 50 million rows the 20 % term dominates, which is why about 10 million dead versions build up before a run.
3. The size the table settles at includes that dead space, so the table looks bloated even though autovacuum is working.
4. Lowering the vacuum scale factor as a storage parameter on just this table shrinks the allowance to about 1 %, roughly 500,000 dead versions.
5. Raising the base or the naptime pushes cleanup later, and replacing autovacuum with nightly VACUUM FULL adds heavy locking without preventing daytime bloat.

lessons.title: Why transaction IDs need freezing
lessons.summary: Transaction IDs wrap around after about two billion, so vacuum must freeze old rows before they look like the future.
lessons.body:
PostgreSQL assigns a normal **transaction ID** (XID) when a transaction needs one, commonly when it first writes. A transaction that only reads never gets one unless it asks explicitly, for example by calling `pg_current_xact_id()`. Row-version headers record which XID inserted them and, if any, which deleted them. MVCC compares those XIDs with the current one to decide whether a version was written in the past (possibly visible) or the future (invisible).

## A counter that wraps around

The XIDs in row headers are 32-bit numbers, so there are about 4.3 billion of them, and the counter wraps back to the start when it runs out. Comparison is therefore circular: from any XID, the roughly 2.1 billion values behind it count as the past and the roughly 2.1 billion ahead count as the future. Newer SQL functions can expose a 64-bit full ID that adds an XID epoch, but row headers still store the 32-bit value.

If a row version kept its original XID while the counter moved more than about 2.1 billion transactions on, it would suddenly look as if it came from the future, and committed data would vanish from queries. This is **transaction ID wraparound**.

VACUUM prevents it by **freezing** old row versions: marking their committed insertion as old enough to be visible to every current and future transaction, so that insertion XID no longer needs normal comparison. Freezing does not lock a row against change; a later update or deletion still follows the usual visibility rules. Even a table whose contents never change must be frozen, because the counter keeps advancing with every write elsewhere in the cluster.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: times on a 12-hour clock
> If a note says "3 o'clock" and it is now 5 o'clock, you assume the note means two hours ago. That only works if you know the note is less than half a day old: a note from yesterday's 3 o'clock would be read wrongly, and one from 10 hours ago looks like "in two hours". Archivists avoid this by stamping old notes "long ago" instead of keeping the clock time.
>
> **How it maps:** clock times are 32-bit XIDs, and half the dial is the roughly 2.1-billion-ID window treated as the past. Stamping a note "long ago" is freezing: the row is then treated as older than every transaction, whatever its original number.
>
> **Where it stops:** a clock goes round every 12 hours whether or not anything happens, but the XID counter advances only when transactions take IDs, so wraparound depends on write activity, not elapsed time.

## Forced freezing and what blocks it

Postgres forces an anti-wraparound vacuum on any table whose oldest unfrozen XID is more than `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` XIDs old: 200 million by default, about one tenth of the 2.1-billion window, leaving a wide safety margin. These limits count allocated IDs, not elapsed time. Anti-wraparound vacuums run even when autovacuum is disabled.

Freezing can only advance past rows that no transaction might still need, so the same things that block ordinary cleanup also stop the oldest XID moving forward: long-running or idle-in-transaction sessions, forgotten prepared transactions and stale replication slots. If the age keeps climbing, the server starts warning when about 40 million IDs remain before wraparound. With fewer than about 3 million left, it refuses to start transactions that need new XIDs, so writes fail while queries that only read continue, until a vacuum catches up.

Monitor the age of the oldest unfrozen XID in each database:

```sql
-- Compare with autovacuum_freeze_max_age.
SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid)
FROM pg_database
ORDER BY 2 DESC;
```

A steady climb towards and beyond 200 million, while anti-wraparound vacuums run, points at something blocking freezing. Find and end the blocker, then let vacuum run; the documentation advises against stopping the server or using single-user mode to recover.

## Key takeaways

- 32-bit XID comparisons look about two billion IDs into the past and two billion into the future.
- Freezing marks old committed insertions as visible to everyone, so wraparound cannot hide them.
- Old transactions, prepared transactions and stale replication slots stop freezing advancing.
- Near the limit, PostgreSQL refuses new XIDs, stopping writes, until vacuum catches up.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: routine vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/routine-vacuuming.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: object identifier types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/datatype-oid.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: system information functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/functions-info.html)

questions.prompt: Why must PostgreSQL freeze old committed row insertions even on a table whose contents rarely change?

options.text: Freezing compresses every table to its minimum file size
options.explanation: Freezing protects visibility across XID aging; it is not a file-compression operation.

options.text: A frozen row can never be updated or deleted again
options.explanation: Freezing records that the insertion is old and committed; later updates and deletions still follow visibility rules.

options.text: Normal XID comparisons have a limited circular ordering window
options.explanation: Freezing prevents an ancient committed insertion from appearing to lie in the future as normal XIDs advance.

options.text: Every SELECT consumes exactly one 32-bit XID
options.explanation: Ordinary read-only work need not allocate a normal XID, while explicit functions and subtransactions can also consume IDs.

questions.workedExample:
1. Normal row headers contain 32-bit XIDs and their comparison order wraps.
2. An ancient unfrozen insertion cannot remain safely ordered forever.
3. VACUUM marks eligible committed insertions as frozen, preserving their visibility as old insertions.
4. Later deletion or update still has its own visibility rules; frozen does not mean immutable.

lessons.title: WAL, replicas and commit durability
lessons.summary: Commit is durable once its log record is safely on disk, and replicas follow that log at their own pace.
lessons.body:
**Write-ahead logging**, or WAL, records changes before the corresponding data pages are written to durable storage. With normal durability settings, commit waits for the required WAL to be flushed; the changed table pages themselves can stay in memory and be written later. Recovery replays logged changes after a crash. A checkpoint writes out changed pages so that recovery need only replay WAL from that point; it bounds recovery work but is not a backup.

This simplified local durability path assumes synchronous commit and normal storage settings:

```flow
Transaction changes buffered pages
WAL records describe the changes
Commit WAL is flushed durably
Server acknowledges the commit
```

Writing one sequential log on commit is much cheaper than forcing every changed page, scattered across table and index files, to disk.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a shop's till roll
> A busy shop writes every sale on the till roll the moment it happens, but updates the stock cards in the back office only when there is time. After a power cut, the manager rebuilds the stock cards by working through the till roll since the last time the cards were brought up to date.
>
> **How it maps:** the till roll is WAL; the stock cards are table and index pages; a sale counts as done once it is on the roll, just as a commit is durable once its WAL is flushed. The last time the cards were brought up to date is a checkpoint. A branch shop receiving copies of the roll and updating its own cards is a streaming standby.
>
> **Where it stops:** a till roll records sales in words, whereas WAL records low-level changes to specific pages. A roll survives a power cut on its own; WAL is only safe once the storage has actually flushed it.

## Settings that trade durability for speed

Two settings are easy to confuse, and their risks are very different:

- `synchronous_commit = off` lets commit return before its WAL is flushed. After a crash, the last few "committed" transactions can be lost, up to about three times `wal_writer_delay` (200 ms by default). The database remains consistent, as if those transactions had aborted. It can be set for one transaction, so only low-value writes take the risk.
- `fsync = off` stops Postgres forcing data to storage at all. An operating-system crash or power failure can leave the database corrupted beyond repair. It is only for data you can recreate, such as a throwaway bulk-load cluster.

## Replicas follow the log

Streaming replication sends WAL to a standby, which replays it. Asynchronous replication, the default, can lag: a user may write on the primary server and immediately read an older value on a standby. A failover can lose acknowledged transactions that never reached the promoted server.

With synchronous replication, the primary acknowledges a commit only after a configured standby confirms it, trading latency and availability for stronger durability. With the default `synchronous_commit = on`, the standby has flushed the WAL but may not have replayed it yet, so a read there can still be stale; `remote_apply` waits until the change is visible on the standby too.

## Key takeaways

- Durable commit needs only the WAL flushed, not every changed table page.
- `synchronous_commit = off` risks losing recent commits; `fsync = off` risks corruption.
- Asynchronous replicas can lag and lose commits on failover.
- Synchronous replication guarantees depend on what the standby must acknowledge.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: write-ahead logging](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/wal-intro.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: reliability](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/wal-reliability.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: asynchronous commit](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/wal-async-commit.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: standby servers and replication](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/warm-standby.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: WAL settings](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-wal.html)

questions.prompt: A user writes on the primary, then immediately reads from an asynchronous standby and sees the old value. What follows?

options.text: The primary violated transaction atomicity
options.explanation: Replica replay lag does not show that the primary committed a partial transaction.

options.text: Every acknowledged commit is already durable on every standby
options.explanation: Asynchronous replication does not provide that guarantee.

options.text: Adding a unique index to the standby removes replication lag
options.explanation: Indexes do not make asynchronous WAL delivery and replay instantaneous.

options.text: The standby can lag; route a freshness-sensitive read appropriately and account for failover data loss
options.explanation: A primary read after confirmed commit can avoid this replica-lag case; asynchronous failover can lose unreplicated commits.

questions.workedExample:
1. The primary acknowledges the commit.
2. The standby has not yet replayed the relevant WAL.
3. Its query therefore sees older state.
4. Define the read-after-write policy and failover durability requirements explicitly.

lessons.title: Backups and point-in-time recovery
lessons.summary: Replicas copy mistakes too; a base backup plus archived WAL lets you rewind to just before one.
lessons.body:
A standby replays the primary's changes, including mistakes. Crash recovery restores logged work; it does not know that a valid DELETE was accidental. This unit separates availability from recoverability.

## Recover an earlier database state

Replication is not a backup. A mistaken DELETE can propagate to the standby. Protect recovery separately:

- A logical dump with `pg_dump` captures one database in a form that can be restored with PostgreSQL tools. Database roles and other cluster-wide objects need separate handling.
- A physical base backup plus an unbroken series of archived WAL files supports **point-in-time recovery**, for example to just before an accidental deletion. The target must be after that base backup finished; you cannot use a backup still in progress at the desired target.
- Point-in-time recovery restores the whole database cluster, not one table. Everything after the target is missing from the restored copy, so a common way to undo one bad DELETE is to restore into a separate server and copy the lost rows back.
- Test restores into a separate environment and measure recovery time. A successful backup command alone does not prove you can recover.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a shared document's version history
> A shared document is mirrored live onto a second screen in another office. If someone deletes a paragraph, the mirror shows the deletion a moment later. To get the paragraph back, you open the version history and view the document as it was at 10:41, just before the deletion.
>
> **How it maps:** the mirror is a streaming standby; it copies mistakes faithfully. The version history is a base backup plus continuous archived WAL, and choosing 10:41 is the recovery target.
>
> **Where it stops:** a document's history can restore one paragraph in place. PostgreSQL rebuilds a whole cluster, usually on a separate server, by replaying WAL forward from the backup rather than undoing changes backwards.

Choose a recovery point objective (acceptable lost work) and recovery time objective (acceptable downtime). Those requirements determine backup frequency, WAL retention, replica configuration and the restore procedure. A managed provider automates some of this, but you still need to understand its retention and recovery guarantees.

## Key takeaways

- Replication can copy an accidental deletion.
- PITR needs a suitable base backup and the required continuous WAL, and restores the whole cluster.
- Test restores against both data-loss and downtime objectives.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: backup and restore](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/backup.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: pg_dump](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/app-pgdump.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: continuous archiving and PITR](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/continuous-archiving.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: WAL settings](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-wal.html)

questions.prompt: An accidental DELETE has already reached the standby. You need the database as it was just before deletion. What is the appropriate recovery foundation?

options.text: Promote the standby and assume the deleted rows reappear
options.explanation: The standby has already replayed the deletion.

options.text: Restore a suitable base backup and replay an unbroken archived WAL sequence to a target before the deletion
options.explanation: Point-in-time recovery reconstructs an earlier state; verify it in a separate environment before replacing the production database.

options.text: Run VACUUM to roll back the committed DELETE
options.explanation: Vacuum reclaims obsolete versions; it is not a committed-transaction undo command.

options.text: Restart the primary so crash recovery skips the DELETE
options.explanation: Recovery preserves committed work, including a valid but mistaken deletion.

questions.workedExample:
1. Replication copied the mistake, so it cannot supply the earlier state by itself.
2. Restore a base backup completed before the desired recovery point.
3. Replay the required archived WAL up to a target before the deletion.
4. Validate the restored state and plan how to handle legitimate changes made afterwards.

lessons.title: Trace latency and budget query memory
lessons.summary: Find where a slow request spends its time, and remember that work_mem is granted per operation, not per server.
lessons.body:
The settings and defaults here are for PostgreSQL 18 with standard build options; inspect the running server before relying on them.

## Find where the time goes

When a request is slow, first separate time waiting for a connection, waiting for a lock, executing SQL and transferring results. Each has a different fix, and tuning the wrong one changes nothing.

- `pg_stat_activity` shows each session's state and what it is waiting for. A session with `wait_event_type` `Lock` is blocked by another, and `pg_blocking_pids(pid)` names the sessions in its way.
- `pg_locks` lists the locks held and requested, for deeper investigation of blocking.
- The optional `pg_stat_statements` extension summarises query behaviour over time when configured.

For a slow event booking, a lock wait on one popular event may dominate even when the primary-key lookup is fast. In a test, a second booking for the same event showed `wait_event_type` `Lock` and named the first booking's session as its blocker for as long as that transaction stayed open. Another index cannot remove the need for competing reservations to coordinate over the same remaining seat count; shorter transactions can.

If the time really is in execution, reproduce the query with representative parameters, examine its plan and check statistics. Then consider query shape, indexes, transaction duration and pool size.

## Budget query memory

Avoid tuning memory or connection limits blindly. The setting that most affects query memory is `work_mem`: the base allowance for one sort or hash operation before it spills to temporary files on disk. Its default is 4 MB. Hash operations may use `work_mem` times `hash_mem_multiplier`, which defaults to 2.0.

The allowance is per operation, not per query or per server. One query can run several sorts and hashes at once, many sessions can run such queries together, and each parallel worker gets its own allowance:

```formula reference
M_sort ≈ wkc
where
M_sort: an illustrative total sort-memory allowance, in megabytes (MB); not an upper bound on server memory
≈: approximately equal to; this budget assumes every listed sort uses its full allowance
w: work_mem, the base allowance for one sort, in MB; PostgreSQL 18 default 4 MB
k: the number of sort operations active at once in each query, no unit
c: the number of sessions running such queries concurrently, no unit
MB: megabytes; PostgreSQL memory settings count 1 MB as 1024 kilobytes (kB)
In words: the worst-case sort memory is roughly the per-sort allowance multiplied by the number of sorts in each query and by the number of sessions running them at once, before adding hash, parallel-worker and other memory.
```

The allowance is an upper limit, not memory reserved in advance; small sorts use little. But it multiplies. At the default, 100 sessions each running three sorts could use about 1.2 GB for sorting alone. Raise `work_mem` to 64 MB globally "to speed up sorts" and the same workload could reach about 19 GB, on top of `shared_buffers` (typically 128 MB by default) and each backend's own baseline memory. That is how a global memory change turns a busy period into an out-of-memory crash.

You can see a spill in `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`. In a PostgreSQL 18 test, sorting 400,000 short strings at 4 MB reported `Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 9976kB`; with `work_mem` raised to 64 MB for that transaction only, it reported `quicksort  Memory: 24788kB`. A hash aggregate on the same rows used about 8 MB of memory before spilling, twice `work_mem`, as `hash_mem_multiplier` allows.

Raise the allowance where you know it helps: for one transaction with `SET LOCAL work_mem`, or for the role running a known heavy report. Limit concurrency with a connection pool rather than raising the setting globally and hoping.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: workbench space in a busy kitchen
> Every cook doing a big chopping job may spread out over up to one workbench; anything that does not fit goes on trolleys in the corridor, which is slower. A head chef who decides "everyone may now use four benches" has not checked how many cooks are on shift, or that each might be doing three jobs at once.
>
> **How it maps:** one job's bench limit is `work_mem` for one sort; trolleys in the corridor are temporary files after a spill. Cooks on shift are concurrent sessions, and three jobs at once are several sorts in one plan.
>
> **Where it stops:** a crowded kitchen just slows down. A server that runs out of memory can have Postgres processes killed by the operating system, which can disrupt every session, not only the greedy job; and unlike a bench, unused allowance is never set aside in advance.

## Key takeaways

- Separate connection waits, lock waits and execution time before tuning.
- `pg_blocking_pids` shows who blocks a waiting session; an index cannot fix contention on one row.
- work_mem is per operation, with larger hash allowances and extra allowances per parallel worker.
- Raise work_mem for a session or role, not globally on a busy server.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL 18: monitoring statistics](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/monitoring-stats.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: pg_locks](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/view-pg-locks.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: pg_stat_statements](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/pgstatstatements.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: resource consumption settings](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-resource.html)
- [PostgreSQL 18: system information functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/functions-info.html)

questions.prompt: One nightly report spills its sorts to disk. A colleague proposes raising `work_mem` from 4 MB to 256 MB in `postgresql.conf` for the whole server. During the day, about 150 sessions run queries that each sort and hash several result sets. What is the main risk, and what is the safer change?

options.text: No real risk: work_mem is one shared pool for the whole server
options.explanation: work_mem is a per-operation allowance, not a server-wide pool. Each sort or hash in each session may use up to that amount.

options.text: Daytime memory could multiply into many gigabytes; set work_mem only for the report's session or role
options.explanation: Correct. Every active sort may use up to 256 MB and hashes up to twice that by default, in every busy session, so memory can exhaust the server. Raising it with SET LOCAL or for the report's role helps the report without changing everyone else.

options.text: The setting is reserved up front, so the server must allocate 256 MB per connection at startup
options.explanation: work_mem is an upper limit used as needed, not memory reserved per connection. The danger is what busy sessions may use together, not an up-front allocation.

options.text: Hash operations ignore work_mem, so only sorts are affected
options.explanation: Hash operations are limited by work_mem times hash_mem_multiplier (2.0 by default), so they can use even more than sorts after the change.

questions.workedExample:
1. work_mem limits one sort or hash operation before it spills to temporary files; it is not a total for the server.
2. A single query can run several such operations at once, hashes may use twice the allowance by default, and many sessions run in parallel.
3. So raising the global value from 4 MB to 256 MB multiplies the possible daytime total by 64, on top of shared_buffers and each backend's own memory.
4. Most of that is only used when queries need it, which is exactly when the server is busiest.
5. Give the extra memory only to the report, with `SET LOCAL work_mem` in its transaction or a setting on its role, and confirm with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that its sort no longer reports an external merge on disk.
